title: Context Memory Fallout — reading notes & experiment sketch
body:
Quick context: getting a coherent narrative to persist across a long multi-turn session is brittle. These notes collect papers, workshop bits, and a concrete micro-experiment plan to probe how and why important facts drop out of a conversation as the token horizon grows.

Topline takeaways so far
- Models often ‘forget’ earlier facts not because they literally delete memory but because attention + softmax weights shift when new strong signals arrive.
- KV cache policies + chunking impact both latency and what the model will actually attend to; eviction choices are a first-order effect.
- Retrieval-style augmentations help, but they change token-budget economics — cost vs. coherence tradeoff is a recurring theme.

Papers / notes skimmed (short bullets, quick impressions)
1) "Persistent Prompts and the Falloff Curve" — workshop handout, NeurIPS 2031 mini-workshop
   - Idea: interleave short persistent tokens every N tokens so the model retains anchor points.
   - Impression: cheap, minimal compute but ambiguity if anchors are overwritten by strong local context.

2) "Checkpointed KV-Store for Long-Form State" (arXiv)
   - Introduces periodic checkpointing of KV windows and a compact replay mechanism.
   - Pros: bounds memory; Cons: replay jitter can cause subtle repetition artifacts.

3) "Latent Summaries as a Router" (poster)
   - Generate compressed latent summaries of each chapter, route queries to the nearest summary.
   - Feels close to RAG but lighter; open question: how to score summary drift over time?

4) "Token Budget Allocation for Interactive Agents" (Systems paper)
   - Formalizes per-turn budget allocation policies (reserve vs. spend-as-you-go).
   - Useful framing for Dedicated vs. Hosted product tiers — different defaults make sense.

Open research questions (brain dump)
- What is the practical half-life of a named-entity introduced at token t=0 in different models (7B/30B/70B)? Measure recall probability vs. tokens since introduction.
- How much does context-window quantization (8-bit kv vs 16-bit) change effective recall?
- Eviction heuristics: LRU vs. semantic-similarity vs. role-based (system/user/instruction) — which gives best downstream task coherence?
- Can we cheaply detect when a fact has 'fallen out' by probing model certainty on synthetic cloze tasks?

Micro-experiment sketch (to run on dedicated infra)
Goal: quantify recall decay curves for small promptable facts and compare caching/eviction policies.
Protocol (fast, reproducible):
- Construct 200 synthetic dialogues (scripted) each ~8k tokens long. Include a set of 3 anchor facts at t=0 (names, dates, single-sentence facts).
- At incremental positions (1k, 2k, 4k, 6k, 8k) insert a probe: a direct QA or cloze that checks presence of each anchor fact. Record model answer and confidence (logits/prob).
- Run across model variants: 7B, 30B, 70B (quantized 4/8 bits where applicable).
- Cache policies to test: no-cache (full context always), sliding-window (last N tokens), checkpoint+replay (periodic snapshot), semantic-evict (vector-sim based).
Metrics: recall@1, token-efficiency (tokens used per successful recall), latency p50/p95, hallucination rate (explicitly wrong recall).

Preliminary hypotheses
- H1: recall drops roughly exponentially with tokens for sliding-window; checkpoint+replay flattens curve but increases latency variance.
- H2: semantic-evict beats LRU when anchor facts are semantically strong but loses when anchors are rare tokens (names).
- H3: smaller models show earlier falloff; quantization accelerates falloff but can be mitigated with smart replay.

Immediate TODOs (for this week)
- [ ] Finalize synthetic dialogue generator (templates + random name/date pool). Ravi to pair on sampling script.
- [ ] Spin up 30B quantized runner on dev-gpu-03 for a quick 50-dialogue trial. (Hannah)
- [ ] Wire probe extraction and standardize answer normalization heuristics (lowercasing, stripping stopwords).
- [ ] Add a simple dashboard: recall over horizon, broken out by policy/model. Can reuse plot template from /confluence/long-context-dashboard.

Notes-to-self (informal)
- Keep probe phrasing constant; avoid conversational paraphrase that opens alternative valid answers.
- Consider both generative answers and logit-based probing (mask/cloze style) — the latter gives a cleaner signal but may diverge from real app behavior.
- Watch for repetition artifacts in checkpoint+replay — log token overlap to detect replay loops.

Ideas for product-aligned evals (how to sell this to PMs)
- Show cost per coherent-turn: how many tokens/$. If Dedicated customers care about sustained sessions (chat agent), tradeoffs matter.
- Define SLAs: e.g., 95% recall of session-introduced identity facts up to 4k tokens for enterprise tier.

Random references / links I should revisit
- short explainer on RAG/latent-summaries (internal repo) — https://github.com/redwood-inference/latent-summaries (TODO: check perms)
- NeurIPS 2031 workshop slides (downloaded) — local copy in /drive/shared_drives/engineering/reading/neurips2031-context-slides.pdf

End notes
- This is messy; that's fine. Primary goal: get an initial data curve that convinces us whether to prioritize caching heuristics or invest in cheap retrieval.
- If results look promising, propose a small internal benchmark and a short tech note for Redwood Console: "context recall curves" to help customers choose defaults.
